articles.title: How Amazon Busts Unions, in Its Own Words
articles.author: Benjamin Y. Fong
articles.content: Nearly ninety years ago, Ford kept its own private security force on the payroll for whenever they needed to beat up union supporters. Having traded in the brass knuckles and baseball bats of the early twentieth century for the empathetic listening and fine-grained surveillance of the early twenty-first, Amazon today employs an entirely different set of tactics to ward off union drives — tactics that may well be more effective precisely because they are so systematic. Amazon is, of course, a notoriously anti-union employer. Though workers at the JFK8 Fulfillment Center in Staten Island voted to form a union in 2022, Amazon has refused to bargain with them, even after the National Labor Relations Board ordered it to do so this past April. When workers at Cornucopia Logistics , a delivery service provider at its DBK4 Delivery Station in Queens, New York, sought to unionize, Amazon cut the provider’s contract. When workers at what used to be the DXT4 warehouse in Laval, Quebec, just outside Montreal, did the same, Amazon not only shuttered the facility but closed up shop in the entire province . Thanks to the disclosure of documents related to its anti-union activity in the province of British Columbia, made available through the filing of an unfair labor practice (ULP) complaint by Unifor, which represents workers at YVR2 in Delta, BC, and is seeking to represent workers at facilities throughout the area, we now have a peek under the hood of Amazon’s anti-unionism. Included in these documents (which were produced in public hearings and not subject to a seal order, and which were provided to me by Unifor) were trainings given to managers about how to stave off organizing drives at their facilities, as well as Amazon’s own list of its facilities where there were active union threats. The picture these documents paint is of a company meticulous and obsessive in its hostility to unionism — an antipathy it has refined into a science. Manager Training Amazon’s employee relations (ER) approach, as outlined in its “Amazon Employee Relations” slide deck disclosed in the document collection, is informed by a wide variety of feedback mechanisms, wherein management can systematically take the temperature of employee unrest. For instance, any employee in front of a computer or workstation device receives a workplace-related “ Connections ” question every day, the answers to which are compiled, analyzed with machine learning models, and summarized for manager review. There are Voice of the Associate (VOA) Boards, where employees voice concerns to senior leaders. Managers also regularly hold “All Hands Meetings,” “Standups” (preshift huddles), and “Gembas” (site walk-arounds), where they are encouraged to listen to their associates. Even birthday parties are framed as an opportunity for feedback. This all sounds very innocuous — what’s wrong with soliciting feedback? — until we get to the very next slide after all of the feedback mechanisms are listed. Here managers are walked through TIPS, an acronym standing for Threaten, Interrogate, Promise, Spy. TIPS are the things that Amazon managers should not do when confronted with a union drive, which include obvious illegalities like “Don’t mention union or you’ll be fired” (Threaten) and “You’ll get that PA position you always wanted if you tell me who is behind the organizing” (Promise). Then comes a slide about FORE (Facts, Opinions, Rules, Experience), which describe the things a manager should do in the face of a union drive. At this point, it becomes clear what all the careful monitoring of the feedback mechanisms is for. Slide from disclosed “Employee Relations 101” presentation. The key “Fact” that managers are encouraged to relay to their workers is that nothing a union promises is guaranteed; the key “Opinion” is that Amazon prizes a direct working relationship with its employees. The “Rules” bit is a somewhat confusing add-on, as managers are simply guided not to change any work rules during a union drive. And the “Experience” part is vague — “share an experience you or someone you know had with a union” — but only a truly confused manager would share a good experience that they or someone they know had with a union. The bit about a “direct working relationship” is emphasized throughout the trainings, and managers are encouraged to cultivate it through a “culture of open communication.” One slide quotes Maya Angelou, who almost certainly never made the quoted statement — “They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel” — to illustrate a good manager’s effect on their employees. This direct relationship is opposed throughout to the supposed way in which a union, Unifor in this case, will “speak for associates.” The lesson Amazon means to impart is something along the lines of: you already have a voice at this company, and the union will take it away. Slide from disclosed “Amazon Employee Relations” presentation. Slide from disclosed “Amazon Employee Relations” presentation. They are also explicit about other things that could be taken away, including overtime, paths to transfer between facilities and promotion, and the company’s “open door” policy. Scripted Empathy The part of the training devoted to manager personability is a fascinating mirror image of labor organizer workshops: managers are encouraged to have “1:1 conversations” where they follow a script but “don’t want to come across as scripted” and listen to their employees with “care and empathy,” “acknowledg[ing] and validat[ing] any emotion . . . in order to reduce the emotional person’s resistance to logic.” They are trained to seek out “informal leaders,” i.e., people “who have influence over their co-workers,” and to not focus on employees “who will never change their mind.” Slide from disclosed “Amazon Employee Relations” presentation. The trainings included in the disclosed documents, including this “Amazon Employee Relations” training, are undoubtedly much tamer than those delivered elsewhere in the world. Labor law in British Columbia is fairly strong, and in one slide of its “Employee Relations 101” training, the company is even explicit that what managers can and can’t say to their employees differs by Canadian province. So in other parts of the world, where managers can be much more strident in their anti-unionism, it’s near certain that the company’s manager trainings encourage as much. Closely Monitored Thanks to the feedback mechanisms described above, Amazon is highly aware of labor organizing campaigns at its different facilities, and it even ranks them according to tiers following the “Atlas” model. Tier 1 facilities are those with active card signings and campaigns, Tier 2 are those “high risk” sites predicted eventually to become Tier 1 facilities, and Tier 3 sites are those where the company considers labor activity possible. There are also lower “risk” Tiers 4 and 5. Sites enter or exit Tiers 2 through 5 based on a mathematical forecasting model that assigns a “Labor Continuity Score” to sites between 100 and 900, 100 indicating a five-alarm labor revolt and 900 low levels of activity. Tier 2 sites are those with a score between 200 and 300. Tier 1 sites include Amazon’s primary North American air hub, KCVG at the Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport; the facilities that Unifor is organizing in British Columbia; and the delivery stations, DBK4 in Queens and DAX8 in Palmdale, California, and the secondary air hub KSBD at the San Bernardino International Airport, at which the Teamsters now have active campaigns. Interestingly, at this time (which I am guessing was roughly two and a half years ago, as it does not yet list the KSBD campaign as affiliated with the Teamsters), JFK8 in Staten Island was not included in Tier 1, though it did have a low Labor Continuity Score of 224. DJT6 in Riverside, California — Amazon’s largest warehouse in the country, which had a ULP strike earlier this month — had the lowest (again, indicating the most risk to the company) Tier 2 score at 223. Again, all of this is based on the feedback mechanisms described above. Amazon knows the key issues that are leading workers to organize at different facilities, and it closely tracks month-over-month “spikes” in worker complaints. Everything entered into the Connections questions or VOA Boards is compiled into closely monitored themes. This is a company that has maximized both worker surveillance techniques and the methods by which they can be exploited to quell labor unrest. While information about how “Employee Relations” resources are deployed according to this information is not present here, one can guess that its ER team pays particular attention to those facilities with low Labor Continuity Scores. Though actual feedback provided is sparse in the disclosed documents, there are legible snippets that speak to a cruel reality at Amazon: while employee comments are closely monitored and synthesized into unintelligible word salads to track patterns of possible labor activity, employees themselves clearly express how their own feedback is regularly ignored. Question for the day!!!!! Does it matter if we the associates voice our views in regards to health issues, safety issues, respect issues, values and moral issues. . . . Fairness and no favoritism. . . . on this platform. . . . it appears that this platform is design so that leaders will know what your concerns are so that they can say, “Well we address the issues” . . . that is before you the associate take the real issues a step higher. . . . Have any of you notice any changes. If you have then God Bless you. Baked In Perhaps the most unassuming of the slide decks included in the collection of disclosed documents is one devoted to a “Leadership Workshop” for facilities in British Columbia. It reviews how to manage “tough conversations” by “leading with empathy” toward “healthy dialogue.” Empathy in tough conversations includes active listening, genuine interest, understanding their point of view, and other affirmable, if somewhat imprecise, suggestions. It all seems quite milquetoast and unobjectionable, until you get to the end, where FORE and TIPS make their appearance, and you begin again to understand what this deck is really about. These slides make it clear that anti-unionism at Amazon is not merely one of several priorities among management. It is baked into the very essence of leadership at Amazon. Managers are trained to listen with “care and empathy” to the explicit end of inoculating employees against union drives. Worker feedback is solicited, not to resolve issues that are raised at particular worksites but to gauge the temperature of labor unrest. These documents portray a company that is not hotheaded and ideological but manipulative and mathematical in its resistance to unionism and willing to deploy the kindest of gestures — care, listening, empathy — in the service of corporate power. While the brass knuckles and baseball bats have been retired, this new, more “enlightened” strategy of the twenty-first century has the same goal: workers scraping by and keeping their mouths shut all so that profits can soar. We’re already starting to see the kind of world that creates, and it’s one every bit as brutal as the days of brass knuckles.

articles.title: Raise Your Hand if You’re Here: Why CDSA Must Intervene in the Board of Education Races
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: As CDSA forges ahead into a busy and demanding aldermanic cycle, membership is set to consider a new slate of potential endorsees at September’s General Chapter Meeting: four candidates for Chicago’s first fully-elected school board. Before those votes take place, I’d like to make the case for why lending our chapter’s endorsement of all four candidates is critical to amplifying our “ Workers Deserve More ” program and furthering the class-struggle messaging that will help build out our movement and propel us to victory in February’s municipal elections. All four school board candidates under consideration ( Hilario Dominguez , Jason Dones , Karen Zaccor , and Debby Pope ) are self-identified socialists who have a clear-eyed vision for what it means to bring socialism to the Board of Education. But perhaps it would be illustrative to first share what the stakes are in these elections; in other words – what we stand to lose should charter and billionaire-backed candidates take these seats instead. Should a right-leaning school board take the helm after November’s elections, there can be no doubt that school closures would be on the table. This would be sold to us under the tired slogans of “fiscal responsibility” and “chronic under-enrollment.” It’s quite the masterful gambit, really. These schools are chronically under-enrolled because of decisions at all levels of government that have left Black and Brown neighborhoods starved of resources for decades. Now, those same actors are returning to demand the closure of schools that they intentionally underfunded. A right-wing school board would likely forsake any attempt at progressive revenue streams from the state. Instead, it would likely close schools exclusively on the South and West sides of the city, just as it did in 2013 . School closures aren’t just about underinvestment. They are a form of violence inflicted on the most vulnerable neighborhoods in this city. They leave communities divested, depopulated, and scarred. Today, the vast majority of CPS schools closed in 2013 remain in disrepair, a constant reminder for neighbors that Chicago has long valued the lives of certain residents over others. Additionally, school closures themselves are often antecedents to violence. Research has consistently demonstrated that areas immediately surrounding closed schools have seen higher rates of gun violence since 2013. Schools are community anchors and hubs where neighbors and their families convene to dream of a better tomorrow – one made possible only by the right to a free, accessible, and comprehensive public education. In many cases, they serve as centers for community programming, provide free summer enrichment programs, and welcome families that have recently arrived to the United States. When families are stripped of that right and forced to send their children to schools miles away at the behest of a school board that’s been bought and paid for by the charter school lobby, it’s an example of how the boot of racial capitalism continues to crush communities of color while enriching their oppressors. How can we seek to grow our presence on the South and West sides under the message of “Workers Deserve More” if we stand by while they’re given less and less? If “Workers Deserve More” is to be an actual vision for the implementation of democratic socialism, rather than a mere rallying cry, it must account for the workers (and their families) most likely to be affected by school closures: in Austin, Garfield Park, Englewood, and Auburn Gresham, among so many other neighborhoods on the South and West Sides. Furthermore, the election of a right-wing school board would likely mean cuts to services for students across the board. The first programs to go would likely be those that support Diverse Learners, students who require special education services. At a time when schools are already understaffed for the personnel that would accommodate these students’ needs (SECAs, paraprofessionals, etc.), it would be unconscionable to consider further cuts. Many students who receive accommodations and curriculum modifications have disabilities. As socialists, we must view this fight through the lens of disability justice. To ensure that every child, in every part of this city, has access to education as a tool of liberation, we must fight to expand funding for our Diverse Learners, not sit idly by while it’s rolled back. While the prospects are quite somber should the school board swing right, there’s also much to be excited about should the board remain aligned with workers and their children. Just as with the City Council, we are fighting to build a bloc of school board members who have proven records as organizers for the working class. These candidates will mobilize the working class to demand the progressive funding for our schools that Governor Pritzker and the Illinois General Assembly have been refusing to answer for . With stable, progressive revenue, we can start to dream bigger. We can work with our bloc of board members to develop a coherent set of policy planks around education that transforms and integrates our schools even deeper into the fabric of the communities they serve. We can begin to imagine a district of Sustainable Community Schools , with wraparound programs like free healthcare, legal aid clinics, and nutrition education. Our district could also fund Universal Pre-K at age 3. Both of these are policies that school board president candidate Hilario Dominguez is running on. It is a program we as a chapter can and should rally around. So in the words of educators across this country: “Raise your hand if you’re here, CDSA.” We need to be here to fully fund our schools. Here to push back against the tide of corporate and billionaire money. Here to ensure that the schools in our black and brown communities are as well-resourced as any school in Lincoln Park or Lakeview, not shut down. And here to dream and organize around a better future for Chicago’s children. articles.title: Russian Elites Are Fighting for Unchecked Power
articles.author: Georgy Birger
articles.content: Ignoring a problem is rarely enough to make it go away. Take civilizationism , an approach based on shared culture taken to the level of civilizational identity. Also called civilization al ism, the idea has been around for centuries and has quietly inspired many conflicts. Overshadowed briefly by Cold War ideological conflict, it resurfaced in the 1990s when political scientist Samuel Huntington famously proposed a coming “clash of civilizations,” in contrast to his student Francis Fukuyama’s suggestion of the “end of history.” Huntington’s thesis was heavily criticized in mainstream academia, partly due to his Orientalism and racialized stereotyping . Still, it had its political impact, even beyond Huntington’s own homeland. After Russia’s conservative turn in 2012, President Vladimir Putin started to call his country a “civilization state,” and the civilizational framing later became central to Putin’s speeches . Similar civilization talk has since spread everywhere from Narendra Modi’s India to Donald Trump’s America . Now that civilizationism is blooming, we can see how its dismissal was essential for its rise. Calling Huntington’s geopolitical vision ignorant, racist, and irrational should not have been the end of the matter but more like the start of the conversation, especially when racism and irrationality were exactly what some adherents of the model were hankering after. As historian Ilya Budraitskis argued , Huntington’s theory was a self-fulfilling prophecy: his ill-motivated predictions gave influential readers, including some world leaders, a useful ideological construct. Russia’s conservative turn, following its “civilizational” realignment, is another example of unfortunate dismissal. The view of Putin’s Russia as an essentially practical-minded actor, which held through the 2000s, obscured the full extent of the changes in the 2010s. Marlene Laruelle, one of the foremost foreign scholars of Russian nationalism, argued in 2013 that Putin’s newly adopted conservative rhetoric on family, sexuality, and national and religious identity was “usually more for pragmatic reasons than ideological ones.” After 2022, though, Laruelle’s own work showed that “traditional values,” anti-Westernism, and civilizational exceptionalism in fact form a genuinely coherent worldview — difficult to disprove given the extent of repression against LGBTQ people in Russia, which goes far beyond a cynical demagogy. Eventually, civilizationism and conservatism in Russia blended into single political force. Thus, in October 2022, Alexander Khinshtein, a member of the Russian parliament (the Duma) justified a complete ban on LGBTQ “propaganda” by framing Russia’s confrontation with the West as “civilizational,” with Russia as the “outpost” defending traditional values. Think of it this way: Fukuyama and Huntington both claimed to describe an era beyond ideological struggle. Yet between them, they handed anti-Western powers both an ideology to fight against (Western liberalism as the last form of universalism) and one to fight with (civilizational identity as its alternative). While some might argue that a global pushback against neoliberalism, identity politics, and Western hegemony was needed, the outcome in Russia’s case — which is now a blueprint for others, including Trump’s America — offers something much worse: a single identity and a culture of absolute authoritarianism that completely deprives ordinary people of power. The New Statesmen and Their Culture War In modern studies of civilizationism, one observation often stands out: how this concept and the word “state” have become entwined. For Mark Bassin of the Stanford-Göttingen Civilizationism Project , “In the Russian version, and maybe in the other versions too, [civilization] can be put together with the state” — noting that for Huntington or his predecessors this was never the case. The statism of the Russian civilizational project was best explained by Putin himself at the 2021 Valdai Discussion Club. Claiming the West could no longer meet the challenges of the present era, he insisted , “Any effective international order should take into account the interests and capabilities of the state. . . . Each state decides for itself how best to protect based on its abilities, culture and traditions.” Meaning, the state is the only guarantor of civilizational identity. The same speech — almost a quarter of it — leaned heavily into culture-war discourse: the “reverse discrimination” against majorities in favor of minorities, “cancel culture” reaching all the way to William Shakespeare, forced diversity in Western cinema, and questions of gender: “Anyone who dares mention that men and women actually exist, which is a biological fact, risks being ostracized.” Putin’s comments at Valdai amounted to saying: the Western way of solving problems does not work for other states/cultures/civilizations, because Western culture is declining. But to fully reconstruct the strategy and logic behind his speech, it’s worth asking what “culture war” actually is. In the modern US context, the most influential definition of a culture war is sociologist James Davison Hunter’s : a struggle between a conservative, traditionalist worldview and one that is secular and progressivist, which over time came to map onto the right and left of American politics, with the rest of the world slowly following a similar path. However, both culture wars and their civilizationism-adjustment predate Hunter’s 1991 coinage. Already in late nineteenth-century Germany, the Kulturkampf pitted liberal nationalists, who framed their campaign against Catholicism as a “struggle for civilization,” against Catholic and conservative forces. A similar conflict played out in the Russian Empire, opposing the secular Westernizer intelligentsia to the okhraniteli (“guardians”) — a conservative-nationalist coalition whose intellectual heirs, Konstantin Leontiev and Nikolay Danilevsky, first theorized the notion of Russian civilization, a successor to Byzantium and adversary of the West. Probably none of this is what you picture when I use the words “culture war” — we think more of online disputes over “wokeness” and “cancel culture,” the flash points Putin raised at Valdai. The final piece of the puzzle is a geopolitical definition of culture war, depicted well by the concept of “cultural victory” in the Civilization video game series. Think of the triumph of Enlightenment ideas in eighteenth-century Europe, credited to France, whose intellectual output dominated the following decades (and spawned German civilizationism ), and the Cold War more recently, which also ended with an American cultural victory. That was what Francis Fukuyama effectively declared in his 1989 “The End of History?” essay: he credited liberal democracy and the free market as elements of Western culture that had proven stronger than the culture of the Eastern Bloc — and so the West had won. Fukuyama’s failure was not so much in declaring victory but in the nuances: crediting democracy as the winner when it was mostly just neoliberalism, and treating the conflict as purely ideological when it was also a contest between two great powers. Or two civilizations, as the North Atlantic Treaty of 1949 stated in its aim “to safeguard the freedom, common heritage and civilisation of their peoples.” With that in mind, it is easier to see “the end of history” as only an interim Western victory. And at the same time, as a revelation for Russia’s security elites: an explanation for their defeat and a hint about how to regroup, by taking the winning culture for themselves. The only complication, given that a culture war had already broken out in the United States, was figuring out which American culture counted as the winning one. That turned out to be easy: in regular statements of Republicans, it was their Reaganite fusionism. That, for instance, was the argument of paleoconservative Pat Buchanan, a former adviser to Ronald Reagan, in the historic speech he gave at the 1992 GOP convention, often considered a moment that brought the culture war to the heart of US politics. Clearly, this choice was not made by some specific, secret group of elites. Most likely, not a single person in the Russian leadership in the 1990s heard any of Buchanan’s speeches. But the following development of post-Soviet culture was largely built on accepting, adopting, and evolving the very same winning culture of free‑market libertarian economics, social conservatism, and blunt anti‑communism that underpinned Reaganite fusionism. A Home Run The post–Cold War anti-socialist consensus not only set the trajectory for the development of Russia’s own fusionism but was also a primary factor in the reemergence of civilizationism in the post-Soviet space. With the Soviet system that leaned on Marxism falling apart, new semantic and theoretical support was needed, which eventually led Russian social science toward the civilizational logic of interwar “conservative revolutionary” Oswald Spengler and the homegrown civilizationism of Nikolay Danilevsky. The civilizational approach offered a shared language for people who otherwise disagreed on almost everything: Western-oriented mainstream scholars and marginalized conservative reactionaries. The main divide was not over the legitimacy of civilizationism but over whether Russia should be seen as part of a broader Western civilization or as a distinct civilization of its own. So, when Huntington’s Clash of Civilizations arrived, it did not introduce anything new to the Russian internal discussion; it was more of a validation: a prestigious Western theorist had finally acknowledged the civilizational fracture it had long insisted on. This mentioned internal tension was, doubtless, already a culture war. In many ways, it echoed that of the nineteenth-century Russian Empire: Westernizers versus Slavophiles; liberals who tried to make Russia an exemplary European democracy versus conservatives who did not believe that possible. Saying that Russia’s own culture war was unrelated to the US one would also be a mistake. As it is meticulously described by Kristina Stoeckl and Dmitry Uzlaner in The Moralist International , the American culture war had already broken into Russia in the 1990s, with the American Christian right going on a missionary quest that contributed to the birth of a conservative coalition in the global culture wars. One example of these practical connections is CoMission, an international evangelical Protestant coalition that distributed brochures in schools and trained teachers in ethics grounded in evangelical Christian values. Its program was eventually shut down by the Russian Orthodox Church, but by that time the underlying morality — the same that had underpinned Reaganite fusionism — had already put down firm roots in Russian culture. In any case, during most of the 1990s the conservatives were neither popular nor united, scattered across different social circles. The “end of history” legend was strong in Russia, and liberals were in control. But then came the severe 1998 financial crisis, which shook part of society’s faith in the liberals, and NATO’s 1999 Yugoslavia operation, which undermined trust in the West. So, when Putin became prime minister in 1999 and then president, he harnessed the resentment. And as he came to power, the reactionaries became united and validated as the opposition to the liberals of the 1990s. In the next few years, a new okhraniteli value system crystallized around Russian uniqueness, opposed by default to whatever Western civilization was — which, as Fukuyama hinted, was liberal democracy. Around that core clustered a cloud of not-always-consistent tags: war with the West, “sovereign” democracy at home, monarchism, imperialism coexisting with anti‑imperialism when the empire in question was the United States, and “traditional values” borrowed from the American Christian right. The opposing liberal Westernizers’ culture was slowly losing its positions — not as fast, though, as liberal politicians were. While architects of 1990s post-Soviet economic reforms like Anatoly Chubais and Yegor Gaidar were heavily scrutinized in the media, liberal culture — which was almost synonymous with “Western‑inspired” culture — largely seemed safe. American movies or British rock music were still cherished by all sides, and all sides wanted Russian culture to be on par. The red lines between liberals and okhraniteli were mostly drawn around gender and religion: some anticlerical exhibitions were shut down, and gay pride events were either banned or attacked by Orthodox and ultraright crowds. Still, the consensus aligned with political scientist John Anderson’s pre‑conservative‑turn conclusion that these were just occasional skirmishes, rather than the makings of a culture war. Then the clash finally happened during the 2011–12 protests over election fraud and Putin’s intentions to return to the presidency. Liberals were mostly the ones protesting, and the statist okhraniteli were deployed to counter them. And as the myth that the protests were orchestrated by Western interference arose, the Western-leaning liberals got branded as traitors. The conservative turn that followed Putin’s 2012 reelection was a counterrevolution. There was no more dialogue with progressive liberal culture, only legislation: like the Pussy Riot trial, the 2013 law banning “gay propaganda,” and the 2020 constitutional amendments defining marriage as a union only between a man and a woman. Consequently, the internal culture war was concluded with mass exile and silencing of liberals and their culture in the 2020s. The Authoritarian International Meanwhile, Putin learned the language of Western culture wars well. When he began preaching “traditional values” shortly after 2012, he was largely reproducing the rhetoric of American hard-right conservatives like Buchanan — who himself asked , “Is Putin one of us?” after one of the Russian president’s speeches. At the same time, Kremlin-linked oligarchs started actively participating in the Western culture wars and spent hundreds of millions fighting “gender ideology” in Europe, while the Internet Research Agency worked to escalate culture-war tensions on American social media. In The Moralist International , an important moment is singled out: a speech that Alexey Komov, a Russian representative of the World Congress of Families (and close associate of hard-right oligarch Konstantin Malofeev), gave at a conference in 2014. “Russia has a real historical chance to become the universally recognized leader of this nascent ‘pro-family’ movement and regain ideological and moral leadership in geopolitics,” Komov said. He expressed out loud what the “cultural win” concept implied: by stepping into culture wars, the Kremlin is seeking global leadership. Starting in 2022, this went from oligarch-funded operations to state policy, while the war against Ukraine was itself reframed as a culture war: “Do we really want, here, in our country, in Russia, instead of mama and papa, to have ‘parent number one,’ ‘number two,’“ Putin asked , explaining the annexation of four Ukrainian regions. Later he signed a decree easing residency for citizens of countries where “destructive neoliberal ideological attitudes are being imposed” — and yes, “neoliberal” in this case means “ woke ,” with a less direct connection to economic strategy. While the way Putin and his statesmen use the culture-war language is almost identical to how Buchanan, Trump, or other US and European right-wing populists do it, there is one major, critical distinction. The latter are trying to harness power in their countries’ internal political brawling, while Russian reactionaries speak as winners of their own inner culture war — which is exactly what gives Russia a chance to rewrite the outcome of the Cold War. Fukuyama’s essay back in 1989 already showed the principle of how this works, when he listed achievements of Western culture that had gone universal, and among them were farmers’ markets and color television. He had a point in context: farmers’ markets in China were an example of the shift toward a market economy, and television culture worldwide really was associated with the West. What this means for today’s Russia is that it did not need to invent a fight against “wokeness” to master and claim it. So, by employing civilizationism, Russia offers an alternative state model that is also, like post–Cold War Western liberalism, universal but allows countries to keep their own culture and traditions. That was exactly what Putin proposed at Valdai in 2021, and during the Q&A after the speech, a certain example arose. Discussing Russia’s negotiations with the Taliban, who had seized power in Afghanistan a few months prior, the Russian president did not exactly praise the Taliban but recognized its legitimacy. “We cannot impose on the Afghan people what the Soviet Union tried to impose, what the United States tried to impose,” Putin added. This perspective reveals Russia’s package offer: people are promised “traditional values,” while elites get a convenient authoritarian system and a seat in the club of the authoritarian international. Russia’s allies today make the pattern obvious: Trump, China, Iran, North Korea, Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, France’s Marine Le Pen — left and right, united only by authoritarianism. Even If You Ignore It Paradoxically, this brings us right back to where we started: the assumption that Putin is a calculating, pragmatic actor. The ultimate goal of his grand culture war is the mundane preservation of power — which democracy stands in the way of. With all that in mind, it becomes easier to connect developments in various culture wars that otherwise look unrelated. Unchecked power is exactly what conservative culture warriors are defending whenever anything threatens to redistribute it: gender politics and trans rights, which strip authorities of the power to define identity and enforce hierarchy; the social sciences that draw on Marxism and critical theory, which make those power structures visible; even climate activism, which leads to holding extractivist elites accountable. Culture wars have always been a battle over the limits of power. What Otto von Bismarck sought in his Kulturkampf was the supremacy of the state over the Catholic Church; what Russia’s imperial okhraniteli sought to preserve was autocracy. State-civilizationism is the same instinct globalized: a libertarian-like solution that looks like a celebration of cultural diversity but is really a claim that no one, inside or outside, gets to hold the sovereign to account — a template available to any ruler who wants the same immunity. Putin, after all, is confident in his ability to survive a world reorganized this way; he is far less confident in his ability to survive his own people. There is no ready recipe for countering this, but one thing is clear: the ongoing culture war that feeds civilizationism must not be dismissed. Distancing oneself from “wokeness,” as some progressive leaders already do , may seem like a smart tactic. The risk lies in letting conservative culture and the authoritarian international behind it evolve unchallenged and unchecked — just like the power it seeks.

articles.title: Cleveland DSA & “The Groups”
articles.author: Cleveland DSA
articles.content: by Martin O. One of the critical questions, if not the most critical and contentious in Cleveland DSA, is our strategic and tactical orientation toward “The Groups.” As we pursue our objectives, where do the many NGOs and activist groups in the metro area fit in? This debate encompasses a variety of political perspectives that have been represented historically for hundreds of years. In fostering healthy discussion of this issue, it’s important to recognize that these positions represent a place in this broader historical political debate rather than simply a particular moral or ethical viewpoint about the value of particular causes. None of the information I’m going to convey here is new; there are no new insights, it’s all available in other places. However, as I’ve been in the middle of discussion with comrades both to the “left” and “right” of me lately (as you’ll see, this terminology breaks down completely at a certain point), I felt it might be important to put all this together in a single post. After all, it’s easier for someone to read one post than 12 and I think it’s essential that comrades recognize the full scope and nature of the discussion and the positions their fellow DSA members hold. This will be about the three most prominent orientations in Cleveland DSA (and really the socialist movement as a whole) toward its direction as it relates to cooperation with outside forces, along with the pros and cons that others have laid out, in the way that I see them. These are, as I’ll refer to them, the “Popular Front”, “United Socialist Front” and, “For a single mass party” positions. These positions to some extent exist on a spectrum of their own that seems to defy the traditional left and right descriptions. Individuals’ positions in this debate are determined to some degree by their personal relationships to these groups around Cleveland and the issues the groups deal with, but there is also an important political assumption often being made in the background around the question of “is DSA one group out of the many groups that an individual might want to do work in and weigh equally?” or “Is DSA the most important group to me out of all of these possible groups?” This assumption affects one’s position on coalitions to a massive degree. There are also questions about the tactics these groups use, beliefs about their effectiveness, their effectiveness in building long-term power, etc. I’ll be upfront that I am a believer in the “for a single mass party” theory of change. Some of this is just because I don’t have the time to be involved in anything other than DSA and my past political activity took me into some of The Groups such as Justice Democrats (not particularly active in Cleveland) and then out of them. My point with this post is to help members understand the perspectives on display so that they can learn to frame questions themselves and we can argue about the politics of the situation and the historical justifications for one approach or the other rather than taking personal shots at each other. Popular Front Popular Front politics, as a historical phenomenon, have roots in the earliest days of the movement for working class political power. A popular front simply means an alliance of cooperation between socialists/communists and liberal political forces, usually against reactionary elements such as Fascists. This is almost always a cross-class coalition between people who depend on wages and people who own capital (in some sense). The working class fought alongside the Republican elites (in the “we want a Republic not a Monarchy” sense) in the 1830 and 1848 Revolutions in France in order to eliminate the Monarchy. In the 1920’s & 30’s, Communists, Anarchists, Syndicalists, and liberals formed popular fronts across Europe to oppose Fascism. Today in the DSA of 2026, many argue that the conditions of Trump’s second term such as state violence and climate change mandate a popular front approach for DSA to orient itself as part of a “movement of movements”. This “movement of movements” would be an alliance of groups all across non-Fascist politics like Indivisible, labor unions, issue/advocacy-based nonprofits, DSA, to Trotskyist groups (maybe, maybe not), etc. Some examples of DSA writing representing this are “DSA For the Masses: Organizing The Anti-Fascist Majority” by Emmett M and “ Coulda, Woulda, Shoulda: A Vision for a Nimble, Mass‑Oriented DSA ” by Chris K of LA-DSA. In Organizing the Anti-Fascist Majority, Emmett writes: “We are witnessing the breakout of large amounts of unrest targeted at the Trump administration, without DSA at the forefront to meet the masses. DSA should support any anti-Trump protest from the Left instead of applying purity tests to them and thereby allowing liberals to control the anti-fascist and anti-Trump narrative….A strong principled Left opposition is needed to stand up to the threat of Trump, and DSA should be at the forefront of it nationally, not standing by self-consciously worrying that we may be mistaken for liberals.” The argument goes that DSA is still a small organization, unable to effectively oppose fascism by itself and that the circumstances demand a unified defense of the American people by DSA acting in cooperation with their allies. Skeptics of this assumption might ask if the popular front itself is even able to cohere the necessary numbers & political power, or question its capitalist character. Proponents of popular front positions might argue however that the actual chance to build a large movement depends precisely on the cooperation with non-socialist forces because DSA is so small and in such an embryonic stage of life, being barely over 120,000 members as of 2026. It follows that the membership of progressive and liberal groups are the closest to DSA politically and the most likely of anyone on the political spectrum to join DSA and build its numbers, which are required to fight fascism. The essential point being made is that the demands of the historical moment or the threat presented by fascism dictate the need to cohere the greatest numbers to oppose fascism in the short term, through a diverse coalition of political perspectives. Critics of popular front approaches such as Jack L in “ Coalitions of the Liberal & Socialist Left” argue that this approach has innate limitations that proponents of popular front politics fail to acknowledge or even ignore, such as apparent historical evidence that the bourgeoisie will eventually betray the working class’s political goals. This manifests in particular ways. In “ Ultraliberalism: The Dominant Tendency of the American Left ”, Chicago DSA member Ramsin Canon argues that the influence of the NGO sector on the left through cross-pollination of membership and the general class position of politically active people means that the socialist movement must fight to maintain its drive to liberate the working class and this requires rejecting the liberal individualist politics of the nonprofit sector that is influenced by competing for funding and the careerism of executive directors. The traditional historical argument such as in Two Tactics of Social Democracy in the Democratic Revolution by Vladimir Lenin says that unprincipled partnership between socialist groups and the bourgeoisie results in the “liquidation” of revolutionary politics to maintain the needs of the coalition. Overall the critical position is represented by a belief that coalitions between socialist groups and liberal groups have inherent limitations. These limitations can be driven by class interests, differing theories of change, disparate organizing capabilities, and competition between activist groups and their leaders, but they represent essential differences between DSA and liberal groups. Points in favor Historically, popular front movements such as in Spain & France have mounted strong opposition to Fascism even if they didn’t always defeat fascism. In Russia, the Tsar was in part able to be overthrown because the national bourgeoisie were tired of him as well. Cooperation between DSA & issue-based advocacy groups has resulted in some huge legislative wins like NYC-DSA’s Build Public Renewables Act. Important electoral wins such as Zohran Mamdani’s in NYC over Andrew Cuomo (backed by Trump) that have energized hundreds of thousands of people Simple reality that DSA is not politically strong enough to get policies passed on its own because this requires legislative majorities or executive power Proponents claim that each incremental reform won allows a new baseline from which to agitate for more changes and which validate the effectiveness of the socialist movement Points against Skeptics say that liberal organizations are more concerned with control of the state in the sense that they can better manage it than fascists, while (as skeptics say) socialists should be concerned with opposing the state as it exists This can take the form of the political horizon being shrunk to simply incremental reforms – this shows acutely on the topics of policing & anti-imperialism Reconciling strategic objectives & decision-making across both liberal groups and DSA can be very difficult when they are structurally so different – mass member democracy vs nonprofits run by executive directors & full-time staff Issue-based coalitions often encounter friction between activist leaders along with mission drift which can lead to wasting time Liberal groups fighting for control of the state / favor with the state might end up shifting their struggle solely to parliamentary concerns or focus just on liberal “consciousness-raising” as Ramsin Canon puts it United Socialist Front As if to address some of the concerns the critics of popular front politics point out, some socialists believe partnerships should only be built with Groups that meet particular political standards such as advocating for police abolition or Anti-Zionism. Operating off a similar assumption that DSA is still a small, still mostly weak formation, they advocate for strategies like running electoral candidates in coalition with other socialist groups like Party for Socialism & Liberation, and using DSA resources to support candidates from those groups. Examples in DSA include the arguments in Akron DSA and elsewhere to support PSL candidates for office and the Springs of Revolution caucus’s strategy of coalitional electoralism. Similar to the popular front argument, this train of thought says that these groups are all “close enough” to DSA and that the demands of the historical moment require us to form the most numerically robust opposition to fascism that we can, except that Zionist groups or pro-NATO groups and such aren’t included. Some of these groups include (but are not limited to) PSL, FRSO, CPUSA (Communist Party of the USA), Socialist Alternative, Revolutionary Workers’ Party, and the Revolutionary Communist Party (of Bob Avakian fame). I personally never bothered until recently to learn what any of these groups were or were about because I came to DSA from the progressive electoral world and I looked at most of these groups as the weird people who just protest all the time and run the occasional third party electoral campaign that gets 1-2% of the vote. In a sense, the horizon for the Socialist Front position shifts from simply opposing fascism to also advocating for socialism unapologetically. However, just as with Popular Front approaches, problems arise immediately because of the nature of the various organizations in the coalition, that often also includes “progressive enough” liberal groups or the front groups that these various sects create in order to appear more legitimate to the general public like the Peoples’ Forum in NYC. This is a reflection of the sect groups’ particular attention to certain historical texts such as Vladimir Lenin’s “What is To Be Done,” which Lenin himself emphasizes is merely a snapshot of a debate at a point in time in the history of Russian socialism, not a blueprint for everyone. The overarching impediment to cooperation between them (and with DSA) is that all of the sect groups believe their organization is the one that’s going to “actually” the one that’s going to cohere the working class against capitalism and the others “aren’t” for various reasons such as their “deviations” in political line. This is a result of the historical development of these groups and the particular interpretations of historical tendencies that they represent, as offshoots of the organizations that came before them. This can include Trotskyists but also Marcyites, Cliffites, Shachtmanites, etc. PSL for example is a Marcyite formation. The question of what to aim for (Socialism in some form) becomes less prominent, although this can be contentious. Instead, the question of how to get there takes center stage. An example of the problems inherent in these sect-type organizations is described in “ The Task of Left Renewal ” by Lewis N in Prometheus Mag talking about the Left in Britain: “The left in Britain has a number of problems – a key one of these is the age problem. Within the British left, there exists a core generation which retains control over the apparatus of the broad left (Stop The War Coalition, Palestine Solidarity Campaign, union branches, etc.), primarily those within their 50s-60s. The problem is not with the participation of these comrades within the movement; it is with their insistence upon leading the movement and stifling the enthusiasm and energy of younger comrades with outdated political culture and processes, ultimately resulting in an insular left which exists simply to remember its past and rest upon its laurels (of which it has little in the past few decades). Younger comrades are consistently tokenized without actually encouraging meaningful participation, resulting in those younger comrades who fall in line with the older sections of the movement out of respect or deference for their history becoming absorbed into the same sectarian struggles which have plagued the left for decades. When we have a situation in which younger socialists are splitting into pre-existing sectarian groups based on their perceived disagreements over their interpretation of historical events for which they were never even alive, and then continue to reproduce the same toxic ideological divisions which have consistently paralyzed the left, we are unable to move forward – only to act as a living museum for those who came before us.” This highlights the primary problem that DSA faces when trying to coordinate strategy alongside these groups. Not only do they solely represent specific niches ideologically, they often are under the control of ruling cliques such as the Becker family that dominates PSL’s central committee. This raises an essential question: are these groups really building a mass movement that can last, or simply a self-serving project of a particular set of activists, usually from a given social class? As we might ask in Cleveland DSA, are they more focused on mobilizing or organizing? Points in favor Generally more revolutionary political line than Popular Fronts that excludes problematic politics like pro-policing and Zionism Preserves ability to have some strength in numbers via cooperation Easier to coordinate agitational campaigning across groups with generally excellent media operations High level of political education across “members” Centralized governance makes for generally efficient operations Not dependent on government or capitalist funding* *exception for Neville Roy Singham and PSL Points against Not really that many people when you add up all the alphabet soup of acronym groups – for example SAlt was ~1000 pre-split, PSL is estimated to be a few thousand, FRSO is estimated to be even smaller Have to argue for membership in your group vs. the other groups – Why would I join DSA who is knocking on my door when the candidate I like that they’re knocking for is from PSL? Can a coalition of this nature withstand the need for freedom of criticism across coalition members when many of these groups exist because they split from other ones or descend from a prior split? Critics say because of the history of these groups they are bureaucratized and controlled by various cliques Emphasis on purity politics and adherence to line means that organizations often split and cohere around charismatic figures and leaders (most famously, splits in various Trotskyist & Maoist groups) “For a single mass party” Finally, I’ll turn to my own camp, the “For a single mass party” crew. A sort of synthesis of both the popular front and the purity politics of sects suggests itself through the failures of the groups Our Revolution that originated from the Bernie Sanders campaign and Justice Democrats that originated in the NGO sphere to recruit progressive candidates. As Bernie said, the regular people of this country today have the historic task of building a mass movement to defeat fascism and demand the democratic republic that we do not currently have, restricted by gerrymandering, campaign finance, the Senate, the Supreme Court, and so on. I have always taken this idea to mean we needed one big organization that would be the standard bearer for the left that people could unify around. Notably, he didn’t say “now all of you go join a bunch of various individual groups like your local Maoist or Trotskyist cell”. It took me years to realize that the missing link was that it had to be driven by member democracy in order to be most effective. Our Revolution never became that organization because it was not based on mass member democracy but run like any other nonprofit around an executive board. But we also need the labor movement to be there too, as the class of society we fight for and whose historic task socialism is to carry out. The classical Marxist merger formula as stated by Karl Kautsky says “Social Democracy [meaning the mass socialist party] is the merger of socialism with the workers’ movement”. So what this “For a single mass party” orientation represents is the project of building that organization, according to its proponents. The “focus on building DSA first” approach views DSA in this light. Supporters of this view of how to run DSA often view DSA, despite its relatively small membership, as a successor to socialist parties of the past and the best shot at a Socialist party of the future. Therefore, for it to be successful requires the organization’s politics and structure to be cultivated carefully into a true party, with conventions, a program like the Erfurt one adopted by the SPD, and so on. In Cleveland specifically, this dovetails with the reverence this crowd expresses for the organizing style of Jane McAlevey in her book No Shortcuts . No Shortcuts , as many would hold, is the key blueprint for building up the organization that merges socialism & the labor movement into a big whole because of its emphasis on building members of the working class into majorities for political action and building individual agency. The main criticism of both the nonprofit sector and the sects that is made by this group is that nonprofits and groups like PSL are all primarily oriented around mobilizing and direct service provision; protests, one-off rallies, harm mitigation, etc. This is in contrast to the mass-movement building that they see happening through organizing in the McAlevey style. But why is DSA the organization most likely to accomplish this out of all the ones that have existed? The answer lies not just in its mass membership democracy but also in Mike MacNair’s thesis in his book Revolutionary Strategy that what is essential to defeating capitalism in the 21st century is a party that harnesses “unity in diversity” across the left. In contrast to the marginalization of the many sect groups throughout the 20th century due to splits and purges, and the absorption into liberal coalitions that the UK Labour party underwent, MacNair advocates for a multi-tendency organization to be the independent political home of the working class, one driven by mass member democracy. Because many of the “for a single mass party” people understand the importance of the multi-tendency organization (not limited to them however), they are some of the most committed to DSA for its own sake. Central to this debate from the perspective of this tendency is what Mike MacNair refers to as the “Strategy of Patience”, the idea that the independent class-based political party must preserve its own political independence and revolutionary character so as to ensure it can build strength and carry out its mission. This means a cautious approach to entering into government coalitions with bourgeois politicians and a cautious approach to partnerships with liberal politics, save for in specific campaigns as a tactic to advance our goals. However, unity in diversity and mass member democracy are not a magic wand. A “DSA for everyone” would seem to replicate the same problems of coalitions, except internally rather than externally. In that sense, it cannot “be” everything for everyone at the same time. Points in favor Emphasis on multi-tendency organizing means new ideas are generated constantly Focus on building majorities within 1 org means able to wield organizational power in a focused way Proponents say avoids pitfalls of popular front politics (risk of liquidation into liberal politics or other organizations) Proponents say avoids pitfalls of sect form of organizing (such as consolidation of power and lack of accountability) because of emphasis on internal democratic processes & structure-building ”Better off together than apart” Points against Can be hard to make decisions among clashing political perspectives Not always responsive to immediate conditions Dizzying to navigate for people joining Critics might say the Strategy of Patience is incompatible with the timetable presented to us by climate change Can lead to strategic flip-flops as different tendencies vie for control of the organization The current composition of DSA is only slowly starting to move toward multi-racial nature and still biased toward a “precariat” perspective, far from fulfilling the promise of the merger formula. But many would say that this represents our best chance so far. Above all, answering the question of how you think DSA should relate to The Groups requires you to clarify what you believe DSA is FOR and how it would be most effective at achieving that. The post Cleveland DSA & “The Groups” appeared first on Democratic Socialists of America .

articles.title: PAC-MEN: The Web of Political Action Committees Pushing Portland To The Right
articles.author: Portland DSA
articles.content: Portland’s capitalist class animates an opaque network of political action committees & non-profits tasked with pushing Portland politics to the Right. In a post- Citizens United world, this incestuous network of wealthy donors and corporations relies on weak campaign finance rules, splashy websites, and endless permutations of the words progressive, Portland, and action! (from Left to Right) Racist real estate developer Brian Owendoff, Andrew Hoan and Jon Isaacs (CEO and Chief Lobbyist, respectively, of the Portland Metro Chamber), and Vadim Mozyrsky of Partnership for Progress/Go, Portland, Go. The Portland Metro Chamber of Secrets The OG lobby of the capitalist class. The Portland Metro Chamber executive committee is helmed by giant multinationals like Bank of America, Amazon, Google, Nike, and Wells Fargo, but it also features local investor-owned utilities, contractors, and health insurers. The Chamber is the main clearinghouse for right-wing candidates who want to hide campaign contributions from the country’s least popular companies, including data center operators, union-busting law firms, and weapons manufacturers. The Chamber distributes money to corporate political candidates through 4 ‘separate’ PACs, which are all headed by the Chamber’s hardest working employee, lobbyist Jon Isaacs. According to campaign finance records, Isaacs is the Treasurer/Director of all four groups. Dishonorable Mention: Working Waterfront is not (yet) a PAC, but the Chamber operates the organization on behalf of major corporate polluters , by fighting against accountability for the dangerous CEI hub and the Portland Harbor Superfund site (e.g. Zenith, Chevron, Exxon, etc). Some current and recent endorsements: State Senate District 15: Janeen Sollman (lost to data center opponent and DSA member Myrna Munoz) Portland City Council: Eric Zimmerman (incumbent), Olivia Clark (incumbent), Steve Novick (incumbent), Eli Arnold (current candidate). Safer Portland, the failed effort to raid the Portland Clean Energy Fund and hire more cops. People For ‘Portland Sucks’ This group is like your co-worker who says, “it’s not political” before launching into a pro-cop tirade about how homeless people are at fault for their circumstances. Rising rents and falling wages don’t come up. These PACs are mostly jobs programs for failed candidates and fired chiefs of staff (e.g. Vadim Mozyrsky, Bob Weinstein, and Eli Arnold, and Julia Brim-Edward’s former staffer, Vikki Payne): Go, Portland, Go Future Portland Partnership for Progress However, their big money originates with some of the largest check-writers funding right-wing politics across Oregon, including Columbia Sportswear head Timothy Boyle. Their steering committees all feature each other’s principal members, according to reporting by the Portland Mercury : “Partnership for Progress donated $32,000 to the new effort, Go Portland Go, in June, according to state records. The organizations also share some leadership; Partnership for Progress co-leader Vadim Mozyrsky also sits on the steering committee for Go Portland Go. The group is also listed as a coalition member on Go Portland Go’s website.” ‘Go, Portland, Go’ attached several famous restaurant-owners to its list of supporters, but this grassroots is already bailing: “Earl Ninsom’s constellation of Thai restaurants—Eem, Langbaan, Hat Yai, Paadee, Phuket Cafe, and OK Chicken & Khao Soi (the latter was erroneously listed as two separate restaurants on the Go Portland Go website)—all appeared on the coalition’s list as of Friday, August 28. But after the Mercury asked about the restaurant’s group decision to join, Ninsom said the company would be withdrawing its support.” Among the restaurateurs still aboard the PAC is the owner of dessert-forward restaurant Papa Haydn’s, which is currently subjecting employees to a nasty union-busting campaign. Landed Gentry Portland’s rent-seekers. Rent-seekers are individuals or organizations that try to increase their own wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions rather than by creating new wealth or providing productive goods. These PACs represent the inheritor class; Portland’s ‘old money’ leveraging vast birthrights to buy property and extract rent from tenants, residential and commercial. Revitalize Portland Coalition Multifamily NW PAC Equitable Housing PAC (statehouse PAC) Portland Metropolitan Association of Realtors PAC The Revitalize Coalition is typical. A pet-project PAC of Portland property-inheritor Jordan Schnitzer, Revitalize bills itself as a “real estate collective” of commercial real estate owners, lawyers, builders, and property managers who want more public money to flow into their pockets. They insist this personal windfall will ‘trickle-down’ to you, despite their twin-objective of cutting public services. This PAC has an extremely high density of Preschool-for-All haters, and they are licking their lips at Julia Brim-Edwards’ persistent effort to degrade the program . Also, unrepentant racist and sockpuppet account operator Brian Owendoff is a Revitalize member : Revitalize’s candidates for the City elections, prior and current, include right-wingers Rene Gonzalez, Loretta Smith, Dan Ryan, Eli Arnold, Olivia Clark, and Eric Zimmerman. On the residential side of wealth extraction, landlord lobby Multifamily NW (aka “Equitable Housing PAC”) collected and distributed over $1,000,000 since 2020 to local and state politicians, across various efforts to oppose rent control, relocation assistance, and free tenant representation. Recent large campaign donations include all of the statewide Democratic Party Leadership (Tina Kotek, Kayse Jama, Rob Wagner, Julie Fahey, and Ben Bowman) as well as Brim-Edwards. Police-Industrial Complex Not much to say here that hasn’t already been said by police reformers and abolitionists for 50+ years. These PACs are funded by cops or by the capitalists who love the cops. “More police” is their hammer, and every social problem is a nail. Increased homelessness? Hire more cops. Grandpa watching too many Fox News ‘Antifa’ segments? Hire more cops? Neighbor’s dog pooping on your lawn? Hire more cops. The PACs: Keep Portland Safe PAC Portland Police Association PAC Community Safety Coalition PAC Portland Police Association Multnomah County Deputy Sheriff’s Association Heavy crossover with the Landed Gentry and the Portland Metro Chamber of Secrets Yet, for a bunch of “law enforcement” officers, they can’t seem to avoid breaking the law. Complainants allege canvassers were instructed to lie to potential voters during the unrealized bid to raid PCEF for cop salaries. The Portland Police Association wasted almost $1,000,000 backing the effort and were humiliated in federal court before finally giving up their campaign. Canvassing Calendar With election season in full swing from now until November, it’s time for the DSA Difference. This calendar is your one-stop shop where you can find all our canvassing dates.

articles.title: Getting Grounded: The Rochester Community Food System Plan
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Elizabeth Henderson First a couple of farm food-related events: “Feeding Tomorrow” – film screening September 23 at 6 pm at The Little , sponsored by the Rochester Food Policy Council. After the one-hour documentary, there will be a panel of local people whose work parallels the inspiring examples in the film. Here is the eventbrite link to purchase tickets – $5, but no one turned away for lack of funds: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/film-screening-feeding-tomorrow-tickets-1994986387990 Tour Mud Creek Farm, a small-scale organically managed vegetable farm in Victor, NY on Tuesday, September 29 at 10:45 am. The Abundance Food Coop, along with NOFA-NY and the Food Policy Council, will be holding a field day to tour Mud Creek Farm to learn about community supported agriculture, and highly diverse vegetable production using organic systems that build soil health and mitigate climate change. Free. Mud Creek’s address is 6880 Cherry St, Victor, NY 14564. The entrance to the farm’s semi-circular one-way driveway is on the north side of the road. You enter on the east end and exit on the west end. The Rochester Community Food System Plan If anyone had doubts, there is now irrefutable evidence that the food insecurity in Rochester’s “Crescent” neighborhoods results from decades of disinvestment, systemic racism and poverty. After three years of work by Consultants KK+P, with guidance from the Rochester Food Policy Council, a 25-member Community Advisory Council, public surveys and focus groups, the City released the Rochester Community Food System Plan (CFSP) on August 14, 2026. The CFSP is “designed to serve as a roadmap to creating a more vibrant, equitable, and resilient food system for the City of Rochester.” The first half of the plan is a solid and realistic report on the history and present state of food and agriculture in and around Rochester with excellent maps as illustrations and cameos of important institutions and individuals. The plan itself consists of five goals, ten strategies and 44 individual actions that can be taken by city government and many partners. Without a movement of working class people that builds the power to take on the underlying injustices of poverty and systemic racism, this plan will not eliminate hunger, malnutrition and food apartheid in Rochester. But it builds on the positive programs that we already have and has many good ideas for more that can be done on our local level. Please take the time to look it over and see where you can plug in. As explained on page 4, “The Plan outlines a coordinated set of strategies and actions that the City of Rochester and its many community partners could pursue to create a more equitable, resilient, and connected food system. Each recommended action includes detailed information with a description and rationale for the recommendation; a potential timeline, partners, and some initial steps to inform implementation; references to related recommendations from relevant, previously completed plans; and any relevant models (with links) from other communities across the country from which to draw inspiration.” The plan presents recommendations in a helpful way dividing them into short, medium and long term, early, keystone and high impact. It also links goals to Plan 2034, a reminder that Rochester has already made a commitment to this work. The plan’s first Goal is to focus the City’s attention on food issues and get the administration to appoint someone whose job it will be to coordinate actions around food and then pull together all the relevant players. At present, like many other cities, Rochester does not have a food department, so anything related to food falls through the cracks or gets shuttled around to several departments leading to confusion and very slow responses. Goal 2 calls for increasing access to healthy affordable food and education about food and gardening. This set of strategies and actions builds on existing programs such as the FoodLink Curbside markets, and also subsidized CSA shares and healthy food boxes with a focus on the neighborhoods suffering the worst food apartheid. An immediate urgent need brought on by the cuts to SNAP funding in the Big Horrible Bill is to make sure everyone who qualifies for SNAP/EBT receives it. Better coordination among the active and caring hunger action and mutual aid groups would help. Equally urgent is making sure that the summer meals program reaches all children, including those who do not participate in congregate programs. As during Covid, mobile delivery vans should be free to give out lunches to youngsters wherever they are. A related effort is to make sure our federal electeds refuse to pass a Farm Bill that fails to restore SNAP funding. The CFSP calls attention to the most critical food apartheid neighborhoods where full-scale grocery stores are few and far between. The City’s “Healthy Grocery” program that identifies smaller stores that carry some fresh produce has not had much effect. Supportive infrastructure is missing such as a reliable service that would deliver fresh food from area farms. There is some fine language in the CFSP that cries out for implementation: “Rochester is surrounded by one of the nation’s most productive agricultural regions, yet not enough of this bounty consistently reaches small retailers, corner stores, and community markets in the city. Building stronger supply chain connections can help ensure that fresh, locally grown food is more widely available and affordable, particularly in neighborhoods facing limited healthy food access. Regional assets such as the Rochester Public Market, Genesee Valley Regional Market Authority, Foodlink, and Headwater Food Hub already play important roles in aggregating, distributing, and retailing regional products. Intentionally creating pathways for urban growers to connect with these distribution and retail networks would help ensure that locally grown food produced within the city itself is part of this supply chain. Strengthening coordination among these actors, while supporting infrastructure such as cold storage, last-mile delivery, and purchasing cooperatives, can help level the playing field for small retailers and alternative outlets. This will expand access to fresh produce, support local farmers, and build community food sovereignty.” A few Rochester schools have gardens and nutrition programs, but most do not. There are enough open spaces on school grounds or near most schools to make it possible for every school to have a garden. What is missing is solid support to encourage and train teachers. The CFSP calls for increased education, but it will take a concerted effort on the part of parents, teachers, and civic gardeners backed up by some funding to move from only a few school gardens to a coordinated program that trains all youth in nutrition and how to grow food, funnels those who get excited into training programs with stipends like the current Taproot programs, and then enables the most committed to access further training crowned by public support to help them access the land and other resources necessary to start a farm. Goal 3 is dear to my heart. It calls for increasing community gardening by building on the network that already exists. Although it took two years of meetings after a crisis when the city bull dozed the Flower City Noire garden, the Urban Agriculture Working Group has made some headway in persuading the city to improve their system for free garden permits that allow for the use of city-owned plots. However, the city still insists that all permits are temporary and can be cancelled if a development opportunity arises. Missing is an agreement by the city to continue reserving some of its plots for development while designating others for permanent use as gardens or greenspace. There is still hope that the final Zoning language will make clear that development is best pursued along transit lines. With over 2000 plots owned by the city, you might think that a few hundred, with a few in each quadrant, could be reserved for gardens. While sceptics are quick to point out that community gardens cannot feed the city, during World War II, “Victory Gardens” grew enough produce to replace the commercial food production that went to feed the troops. We can do this! With climate disaster and a just-in-time corporate-dominated food system that crumbles when a crisis hits, it behooves us here in Rochester to take our gardens and local farms more seriously. The City’s Recreation and Human Services department already has a good program staffed by people who actually know how to grow things with gardens and training at rec centers and annual deliveries of plants and other supplies to community gardens. There is a solid base to start from. Goal 4 aims at strengthening the connections between the city and the highly fertile and productive farms in the Finger Lakes counties starting with more investments in the Public Market as the food development center for the city. Although it scores as one of the outstanding markets in the whole country, the Rochester Public Market suffers from persistent understaffing and improvements move slowly. Hopefully the CFSP will bring it the attention it deserves. More support for Headwater Foods so that it can move into the city and expand is another promising set of actions. The plan also points to institutional purchasing of NY grown foods as a way improve local diets. The Good Food Bill, an important piece of legislation that would allow public institutions like schools to pay up to 10% more to “values-based” NY farm suppliers, sits on Governor Hochul’s desk awaiting signature. It is taking a major statewide campaign to get her to sign (another story for another time). Sadly, the Rochester School District has not taken advantage of the existing state and federal programs that increase funding for schools that buy from farms. RCSD is leaving a lot of money on the table that could improve school lunches. Since I did not grow up in Rochester nor did my son, I have left it to others on the Food Policy Council committee who had this experience to try to address this extremely frustrating and intransigent situation. In the plan’s reporting on the existing Rochester food system, there is solid data on the 10% of city jobs that are food-related. One small portion of those jobs are the small food enterprises that attract people with the chance to run their own businesses and produce something creative. Action 4B-1 rightly rates support for these entrepreneurs as a possible “early win,” and adding incentives to the rfps for city-provided grants to developers to include space for gardens and food businesses should be a measure the city development department could take on immediately. 4B 2, 3 and 4 have good proposals for a series of ways the city can support food enterprises. The CFSP also documents the low wages and poor working conditions of the hundreds of food-related jobs in retail, fast foods, and groceries and even includes data about the small percentage that are unionized and pay better, but fails to include actions, such as union drives and contracts, that might transform them into living wage jobs. Sweet as it is, enabling a home jam artist to parlay her skills into a small business will not reduce poverty and hunger. 4C 4 links training programs to food enterprises, but does not include training as a union organizer among the skills most needed. No one can argue with Goal 5: “Celebrate the diverse human, cultural, and natural assets of Rochester and the Finger Lakes region by leveraging the power of food to build connection and strengthen community.” The authors of the plan have combed the country for lots of good suggestions for how to do this. There is one action that I hope the Food Policy Council will take up soon – to hold an annual or biannual food summit to gather everyone involved in implementing the plan to assess progress and make further plans together. … As someone who spends so much of my time and energy on food – growing it, harvesting it, cooking and eating it, teaching others how to grow it, organizing around it, writing about it – my hope is that the CFSP will attract more attention to the shockingly unjust state of food in our city and inspire some action for change.
